questions.stem: The SOUTH-WEST MONSOON normally arrives over the Kerala coast on:
questions.explanation: SW MONSOON ONSET over Kerala — NORMAL DATE = 1 JUNE (declared by India Meteorological Department, IMD). IMD officially declares onset based on FIVE OBJECTIVE CRITERIA (since 2006): (1) 60%+ of 14 designated stations in Kerala-Lakshadweep region receive rainfall ≥ 2.5 mm for 2 consecutive days after 10 May; (2) Westerly wind depth ≥ 6 km with speeds 15-20 knots at 925 hPa; (3) Outgoing Long-wave Radiation (OLR) below 200 W/m²; (4) Cloud cover increase; (5) Wind direction WSW-SW. MONSOON PROGRESSES NORTHWARD thereafter: Mumbai ~10 June; Kolkata ~8 June; Delhi ~29 June; reaches entire country by ~15 JULY. WITHDRAWAL (retreat) begins from NW India around 1 SEPTEMBER, complete withdrawal from entire country by ~15 October. DURATION: SW monsoon gives ~75% of India's annual rainfall in 4 months (June-Sep). ANOMALIES: Onset delay of more than 7 days → impacts kharif sowing, drought risk. El Niño years typically weaken monsoon; La Niña strengthens it. 2023 = 'below normal' monsoon (El Niño); 2022 = 'normal'. LGP (Long-Period Average) rainfall = ~880 mm; 'normal' = 96-104% of LPA. normal onset date declared by IMD.

questions.stem: The Indian SW Monsoon splits into two branches after striking the southern tip of peninsular India — the ARABIAN SEA BRANCH and the:
questions.explanation: SW MONSOON — TWO BRANCHES: (1) ARABIAN SEA BRANCH — hits the Western Ghats, causes HEAVY rainfall on windward side (Mahabaleshwar, Mangaluru, Kochi); crosses the Ghats creating RAIN SHADOW on leeward Deccan Plateau (Pune gets ~700mm vs Mumbai ~2200mm). Sub-branches continue to Gujarat + Rajasthan + Punjab (light rain). (2) BAY OF BENGAL BRANCH — strikes Myanmar coast + Arakan Yoma + deflects towards Ganga plains; Assam + NE India receive VERY HEAVY rainfall (Mawsynram + Cherrapunji = wettest places on Earth, ~11,800+ mm/yr). Branch moves WESTWARD along Himalayan foothills causing rainfall in UP, Bihar, Punjab (reaches Punjab around end of June). The TWO BRANCHES MEET over NW India (Punjab + Haryana). MECHANISM: Differential heating of land + sea; ITCZ shifts northward to ~25°N in summer; low pressure over Indian subcontinent draws moisture-laden SE trade winds from southern hemisphere that cross equator + deflect RIGHT (NW direction) as per Coriolis — becoming SW winds hitting India. Also driven by Tibetan Plateau heating + Tropical Easterly Jet.

questions.stem: MAWSYNRAM in Meghalaya holds the record for the HIGHEST ANNUAL RAINFALL in the world. The reason it out-rains Cherrapunji is:

options.option_text: It is closer to the sea
It is at a higher elevation and its conical hills FUNNEL the Bay of Bengal monsoon branch into a narrow valley, forcing greater orographic uplift

questions.explanation: MAWSYNRAM (East Khasi Hills, Meghalaya) — HIGHEST ANNUAL RAINFALL in the world, ~11,871 mm average (some years 15,000+ mm). Just ~15 km from Cherrapunji (Sohra) which records ~11,777 mm — they swap the 'wettest place' title year to year. WHY SO WET: (a) Bay of Bengal branch of SW Monsoon sweeps up moisture-laden air over Bangladesh plains; (b) hits the KHASI HILLS abruptly (south-facing scarp); (c) OROGRAPHIC UPLIFT — moist air forced to rise rapidly, cools, condenses as torrential rain; (d) Mawsynram's CONICAL HILLS form a natural funnel, concentrating clouds into a narrow valley (Cherrapunji, slightly lower elevation, lacks this funnel). RESULT: clouds are literally squeezed dry over these hills. SEASONAL DISTRIBUTION: ~90% of annual rainfall falls June-September. CHERRAPUNJI RECORDS: 9,300 mm in July 1861 (highest monthly); 26,470 mm in 1860-61 (highest annual worldwide). IRONY: despite highest rainfall, both villages face DRINKING WATER SCARCITY in dry months — steep slopes + deforested terrain cause rapid runoff; local people rely on bamboo-pipe rainwater harvesting. Also home to LIVING ROOT BRIDGES of the Khasi + Jaintia tribes (figus elastica roots trained across streams — can last 500+ years).

questions.stem: The RAIN-SHADOW effect of the Western Ghats means the LEEWARD side (eastern slopes + Deccan) receives much less rainfall. Which city represents this rain-shadow?
questions.explanation: RAIN-SHADOW EFFECT — when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier, it cools + drops rainfall on the WINDWARD side; by the time it descends on the LEEWARD side it is dry + warm (adiabatic warming). WESTERN GHATS + SW MONSOON example: (a) WINDWARD (western coast) — very wet: MUMBAI ~2200 mm, MANGALURU ~3500 mm, KOCHI ~3000 mm, AGUMBE/KUDREMUKH (Karnataka) ~7500 mm — 'Cherrapunji of the South'. (b) LEEWARD (eastern, Deccan) — dry: PUNE ~700 mm, AHMEDNAGAR ~550 mm, SOLAPUR ~720 mm, BELLARY ~550 mm. This rain-shadow is why MARATHWADA + parts of KARNATAKA'S EASTERN DRY ZONE are chronically drought-prone. The belt through which the monsoon passes BEFORE releasing its moisture is the 'Desert belt of the Deccan'. ANANTAPUR (Andhra Pradesh) — only ~550 mm — is India's SECOND-DRIEST DISTRICT (Jaisalmer being driest). Note: NE monsoon (Oct-Dec) partly compensates the Tamil Nadu + Rayalaseema coastal rain-shadow, giving them another shot at rain. AURANGABAD gets 725mm. 'LEEWARD' = downwind side; 'WINDWARD' = upwind side. ~700mm annual vs Mumbai's ~2200mm — just 150km away, on the leeward side of the Ghats.

questions.stem: The NORTH-EAST (retreating) MONSOON is the main source of rainfall for:

options.option_text: TAMIL NADU, COASTAL ANDHRA, RAYALASEEMA, Puducherry (Oct-Dec)

questions.explanation: NE (RETREATING) MONSOON = WINTER MONSOON = post-monsoon season (October-December). As the ITCZ retreats southward, WINDS reverse from SW to NE, picking up moisture from the Bay of Bengal as they blow over it. Hits the EAST COAST of India. BENEFICIARIES: (1) TAMIL NADU — gets ~60% of its ANNUAL rainfall during NE monsoon (Nov-Dec); Chennai floods of Nov-Dec are a regular feature. (2) COASTAL ANDHRA PRADESH + RAYALASEEMA. (3) SOUTHERN KARNATAKA (coastal parts) + PUDUCHERRY. (4) SOUTH KERALA + SRI LANKA get some rain too. TAMIL NADU is UNIQUE — during SW monsoon it's in rain-shadow of the Western Ghats + gets very little rain, so it depends on NE monsoon + cyclones for water supply. CYCLONES — Oct-Dec is the peak season for Bay of Bengal cyclones hitting east coast (Tamil Nadu, AP, Odisha, WB, BD). WITHDRAWAL: NE monsoon wanes by early January; December is transitional. SW MONSOON = moist; NE MONSOON = drier overall (except coastal TN) because winds originate from cool, dry continental Asia (Siberian high). The NE monsoon phenomenon is called 'CHENNAI RAINS' colloquially. rain-shadow of SW monsoon.

questions.stem: EL NIÑO is a climatic phenomenon associated with:

options.option_text: Abnormal WARMING of Pacific Ocean surface waters

questions.explanation: EL NIÑO — Spanish for 'the little boy' / 'Christ child' (so named by Peruvian fishermen because it peaks around Christmas). Part of the ENSO (El Niño-Southern Oscillation) cycle. MECHANISM: Normally, TRADE WINDS blow east-to-west across the Pacific, piling warm water in the western Pacific (Indonesia + Philippines) + allowing cold water upwelling off Peru. In EL NIÑO years, trade winds WEAKEN/REVERSE, warm water sloshes eastward, Peruvian coast sees ANOMALOUS WARM surface temperatures (+0.5°C to +3°C). GLOBAL IMPACT: drought in Australia + Indonesia; floods in Peru + California; bleaches coral reefs (2016, 2023 bleaching events). INDIAN MONSOON LINK: El Niño → HADLEY + Walker cells disrupted → descending dry air over Indian subcontinent → WEAKER/DELAYED SW monsoon. 60% of El Niño years since 1900 have had below-normal Indian rainfall (drought). Recent El Niño years: 1997-98 (strong), 2015-16 (strongest on record), 2023-24 (moderate — led to 5% below-normal Indian rainfall). LA NIÑA (opposite) — Pacific cooling; STRENGTHENS Indian monsoon typically. 2020-22 was a rare 'triple-dip' La Niña → good monsoons. Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) — local analog; positive IOD offsets El Niño effect. typically WEAKENS the Indian SW monsoon; around Peru + Ecuador.

questions.stem: The 'BURSTING of the monsoon' refers to:

options.option_text: The SUDDEN, heavy onset of SW monsoon rainfall, marking the transition from dry pre-monsoon to active monsoon regime

questions.explanation: 'BURST OF MONSOON' — the SUDDEN + VIGOROUS arrival of the SW monsoon rains after weeks of oppressive pre-monsoon heat + humidity. Characterised by: (1) sharp drop in temperature (5-8°C overnight); (2) dark thunderclouds + torrential rain that can last days; (3) gusty winds from the SW; (4) sudden green-up of vegetation. Kerala experiences the FIRST BURST ~1 June. FROM the burst onwards, the monsoon is in 'active' mode. PRE-MONSOON SHOWERS (not the burst): (a) MANGO SHOWERS (Apr-May) — pre-monsoon thunderstorms in Kerala + Karnataka, helping ripen mangoes (hence the name). (b) BLOSSOM SHOWERS (Apr-May) — Karnataka coffee belt, help coffee flower. (c) KAAL BAISAKHI / NOR'WESTERS — violent thunderstorms in Bengal + Assam in April-May; called 'Bardoli Chheerha' in Assam; locally feared but beneficial for jute + rice. (d) LOO — hot dry WINDS (not rain) in N India during May-June; heat waves. (e) CHERRY BLOSSOM SHOWERS — Karnataka coffee. 'BREAKS IN MONSOON' (not burst) — dry spells within the active monsoon period; common + sometimes prolonged, can cause drought even in a 'normal' monsoon year.

questions.stem: The JET STREAM most relevant to Indian monsoon onset is the:
questions.explanation: JET STREAMS + INDIAN MONSOON: (1) SUBTROPICAL WESTERLY JET (STWJ) — winter jet at ~30°N, sits SOUTH of the Himalayas in winter; brings western disturbances (winter rain to N India). In May-June, STWJ MIGRATES NORTH of the Himalayas → low-level easterlies + SW monsoon can establish. The 'retreat' of STWJ is a KEY TRIGGER for monsoon onset (called the 'monsoon onset vortex'). (2) TROPICAL EASTERLY JET (TEJ) — summer jet; upper-tropospheric easterly at ~100-200 hPa, centered around 15°N; flows from SE Asia across India to Africa. Strong TEJ in June → strong divergence aloft → helps drive surface convergence + heavy rainfall. WEAK TEJ = weak monsoon. DISCOVERY: TEJ was first described by P. Koteswaram (1958), an IMD scientist. TIBETAN PLATEAU HEATING: reinforces TEJ by creating a warm anticyclone aloft over Tibet. MADDEN-JULIAN OSCILLATION (MJO) — eastward-moving tropical disturbance; modulates monsoon on 30-60 day timescale — 'active' + 'break' phases of monsoon partly driven by MJO passage. WALKER CELL + HADLEY CELL are zonal + meridional circulations, not jet streams per se. WESTERN DISTURBANCES come from Mediterranean via STWJ in winter.

questions.stem: The INDIAN OCEAN DIPOLE (IOD) when POSITIVE is associated with:

options.option_text: Caused by Pacific trade winds only

questions.explanation: INDIAN OCEAN DIPOLE (IOD) — first identified in 1999 by scientists at JAMSTEC (Japan). Measured as SST (sea-surface temperature) difference between the WESTERN (off Somalia/Arabia) and EASTERN tropical Indian Ocean (off Sumatra). POSITIVE IOD (+IOD): west is ANOMALOUSLY WARM, east is COOLER than normal. Consequences: (a) warmer western Indian Ocean boosts moisture content near Indian subcontinent → STRENGTHENS SW monsoon; (b) drought-like conditions in Indonesia + Australia (2019 Australian bushfires linked to strong +IOD); (c) can OFFSET El Niño's weakening effect — e.g., 1997 saw concurrent strong El Niño + strong +IOD, India got NORMAL rainfall (El Niño alone would have caused drought). NEGATIVE IOD (-IOD) — opposite; typically weakens monsoon. INDICATOR: Dipole Mode Index (DMI) = SST(West) - SST(East); DMI > +0.4°C = positive IOD event. DURATION: IOD events last ~3-6 months, typically peak Aug-Oct; don't persist like ENSO. Other oceanic drivers of Indian monsoon: ENSO (Pacific), Atlantic Niño, Madden-Julian Oscillation, Indian Ocean Warm Pool. PREDICTION: IMD uses IOD forecast as one input in its monsoon forecast model. Positive IOD years: 1994, 1997, 2006, 2015, 2019, 2023. warmer western Indian Ocean (off Somalia/Arabia) + cooler eastern side (off Indonesia) → enhanced moisture transport to India.

options.option_text: Heavy rain that destroys mango crops
PRE-monsoon thunderstorm showers in KERALA + coastal KARNATAKA (April-May) that help mangoes ripen
A variety of shower trees in Kerala

questions.explanation: MANGO SHOWERS (KERALA) / BLOSSOM SHOWERS (KARNATAKA) — PRE-MONSOON thunderstorms during April-May on the west coast of peninsular India. Triggered by: afternoon convective heating of land → rising hot air → condensation → brief but intense thunderstorms. EFFECT: help MANGO FRUITS ripen (hence 'mango showers') + help COFFEE BEANS flower ('blossom showers'). Similar pre-monsoon local thunderstorms elsewhere in India: (1) NOR'WESTERS / KAAL BAISAKHI — violent thunder-squalls in West Bengal + Assam (April-May), locally feared for damage but bring rain for rice + jute. In Assam also called 'BARDOLI CHHEERHA'. (2) LOO — hot dry continental winds (April-June) across N India + Pak; can be 45-50°C, cause heat-stroke. 'Loo' is NOT a shower. (3) CHERRY BLOSSOM SHOWERS — Karnataka coffee plantations. CATEGORY: all these are 'local winds + weather phenomena' — a favourite SSC/UPSC GS-1 category. Other LOCAL WINDS globally: Chinook (N America, 'snow-eater'), Foehn (Alps), Sirocco (Mediterranean), Mistral (France), Harmattan (W Africa), Bora (Adriatic), Santa Ana (California), Khamsin (Egypt), Brickfielder (Australia).
